paper_title: Reframe: Observation-Aligned Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation for Agentic Visual Reasoning

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) and multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) offer complementary routes to post-training. For visual agents, however, tool use presents two related challenges. Models may overlook useful tool-returned observations, while poorly grounded actions can limit the evidence available for subsequent distillation. We introduce Reframe, a post-training framework that treats the observation state, rather than only the output distribution, as an object of alignment. First, Ground-Drop-GRPO (GD-GRPO) trains spatial and temporal specialists with evidence-aware rewards and stochastic removal of the original visual input, encouraging them to acquire grounded evidence and use the returned observations. Second, Observation-Gated-MOPD (OG-MOPD) replaces deficient tool actions with canonical ones mid-rollout and resumes distillation from the repaired observation. The two stages complement each other, as learning to rely on tool-returned observations can help the policy benefit from observation repair. Neither stage requires a task-specific SFT cold start. Extensive experiments over 14 image and video benchmarks demonstrate that Reframe outperforms both Mix-RL and vanilla MOPD. Ablation results show that GD-GRPO increases observation dependence and tool gain compared with outcome-based GRPO.

sections.content: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) and multi-teacher onpolicy distillation (MOPD) offer complementary routes to post-training. For visual agents, however, tool use presents two related challenges. Models may overlook useful toolreturned observations, while poorly grounded actions can limit the evidence available for subsequent distillation. We introduce Reframe, post-training framework that treats the observation state, rather than only the output distribution, as an object of alignment. First, Ground-DropGRPO (GD-GRPO) trains spatial and temporal specialists with evidence-aware rewards and stochastic removal of the original visual input, encouraging them to acquire grounded evidence and use the returned observations. Second, Observation-Gated-MOPD (OG-MOPD) replaces deficient tool actions with canonical ones mid-rollout and resumes distillation from the repaired observation. Ablation results show that GD-GRPO increases observation dependence and tool gain compared with outcome-based GRPO. https://github.com/EliYuan30/Reframe 1. Introduction Agentic visual reasoning addresses the evidence-sparse bottleneck in perception-centered tasks by equipping visionlanguage models (VLMs) with tools to acquire fine-grained evidence. Related studies include think with images [13, 25, 3234, 47, 48] and think with videos [12, 28, 41, 45]. However, invoking tool does not guarantee that the model uses what it returns. We term this problem observation neglect, where model acquires an intermediate observation but its subsequent reasoning is largely unaffected [37]. Alongside efforts to improve when tools are invoked [33, 34, 42], this Figure 1. Overview of Reframe: visual agents should produce reliable intermediate results and truly look at them. (a) Outcome-based RL without explicit grounding rewards can permit observation neglect. (b) Vanilla MOPD may supervise trajectories conditioned on poorly grounded observation state. (c) Our GD-GRPO rewards grounded actions and encourages reliance on tool-returned observations. (d) Our OG-MOPD repairs deficient tool actions before continuing distillation. raises complementary question of how to train models to make effective use of the acquired observation. Meanwhile, most previous works focus exclusively on single modality, while the few that simultaneously incorporate image and video tools rely on mixed-data SFT-thenRL training paradigm. However, this often leaves the final unified model significantly lagging behind the one trained on single modality. We argue that this is the combined result of the pattern conflict of off-policy SFT training and the supervision sparsity of RL. more promising alternative is densely supervised, predominantly on-policy training paradigm. On-policy distillation (OPD) serves as foundational approach: by supervising the students own rollouts with dense token-level feedback, it bypasses both the sparse credit assignment of RL and the reference bias of off-policy imitation [1, 31]. Extending this paradigm, multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) [24] routes student-generated trajectories to domain-specialized teachers, and has been increasingly adopted by frontier models [4, 5, 14, 23, 44]. Subsequent works further refine it in 1 Table 1. Comparison with representative visual agents. Reframe adopts predominantly on-policy paradigm to consolidate image and video reasoning within unified model, while achieving the highest observation dependence and tool gain among the compared models. Observation dependence is measured on V. Tool gain is measured across seven image benchmarks. Model Pixel-Reasoner Thyme DeepEyes DeepEyesV2 Reframe (Ours) Training Properties Effective Tool Use Unified ImageVideo No SFT Cold Start Observation Dependence Tool Gain 23.25 34.20 19.47 41. 75.53 +0.97 +1.47 +1.32 2.45 +5.23 terms of capability imbalance [11], heterogeneous convergence [2], behavioral drift under tool use [29], and crossmodal routing [20, 27]. However, existing paradigms primarily refine how supervision is delivered without intervening in rollout trajectories. This is critical limitation for agentic visual reasoning since subsequent supervision is all conditioned on what tools returned. Motivated by these, we propose Reframe, twostage training framework comprising Ground-DropGRPO (GD-GRPO) and Observation-Gated-MOPD (OG-MOPD). Together, the two training stages enforce the two core properties for effective tool use: GD-GRPO makes the acquired observation necessary, while OGMOPD keeps it valid. GD-GRPO directly targets the neglect problem by augmenting observation-based reward and stochastically dropping the original visual input. It forces the model to genuinely rely on the tool-returned results. Subsequently, OG-MOPD ensures that consolidation remains conditioned on valid trajectories by repairing deviated tool use. Across 14 image and video benchmarks, Reframe outperforms both Mix-RL and vanilla MOPD, even surpassing the dedicated experts on average. Furthermore, diagnostic analyses on observation dependence confirm that Reframe exhibits markedly stronger causal reliance on tool-returned results than previous methods. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We propose Reframe, the first tool-use MOPD framework that unifies image and video agentic reasoning. Its OG-MOPD actively intervenes in rollout trajectories and repairs deviated tool actions, promoting observation validity throughout cross-modal consolidation. We address observation neglectthe issue where agentic VLMs invoke tool yet overlook what it returns. Through GD-GRPO, we enforce observation necessity via input dropping and observation rewards. We develop the Reframe-100K dataset to support both training stages. Evaluations across 14 image and video benchmarks show consistently improved performance. Code, dataset, and model are open-sourced. 2. Related Work Agentic visual reasoning. Multimodal reasoning often uses textual chain-of-thought (CoT) [6, 7], but its benefits vary across visual tasks [9, 22, 43]. Recent approaches instead incorporate visual information into reasoning [16, 25], including interfaceor code-based tool calls that acquire query-relevant observations. These tools allow models to inspect image regions and video segments in finer detail that may be difficult to resolve from the original input. However, acquiring finer visual evidence does not guarantee its use. Recent studies find that tool-returned observations may have little causal effect on subsequent predictions [26, 37]. On-policy distillation. OPD provides dense token-level feedback on student-generated rollouts, reducing the statedistribution mismatch of off-policy imitation [1, 31]. Effective transfer depends on compatible reasoning and novel teacher capabilities [19], coverage of student-visited states [10], and teacher corrections within the students learnable token support [36]. Extensions support blackbox teachers through logit-free verification [50], temporal video grounding [17], and supervision through teachergenerated reasoning steps [39]. These methods primarily refine supervision along student-generated trajectories. For visual agents, however, preceding tool actions also determine which observations are available when that supervision is applied. Token-level feedback on continuation cannot retroactively recover evidence that the preceding action failed to acquire. Multi-teacher on-policy distillation. MOPD consolidates independently trained specialists by routing teacher supervision over shared students rollouts [24], an approach increasingly used in frontier-model post-training [5, 14, 23, 44]. Open-MOPD studies imbalance from token budgets, convergence drift, and stale supervision [11], while D3-MOPD adapts domain sampling to different convergence rates [2]. Multimodal variants route specialists for GUI interaction and video understanding [20, 27]. Other work identifies distortions of decision-critical tool tokens despite sufficient retained teacher probability mass [29]. These advances focus on routing and supervision while generally taking rollout observations as given. Reframe instead considers both whether acquired observations are used and whether they provide valid evidence for subsequent distillation, supporting unified image and video reasoning. 3. Method In this section, we introduce the data construction and the two-stage training procedure of Reframe. We make three 2 we derive tool-applicability labels from annotation coverage, distinguishing beneficial, neutral, and non-beneficial examples without relying on base-model rollout accuracy or stronger-model judgments of tool utility. This avoids introducing model-prediction bias into applicability labels. Importantly, examples are not discarded solely because the base model can answer them without tools, as even correctly answered questions can provide valuable spatial or temporal tool-use supervision. Context-aware evidence. Grounding annotations typically localize minimal objects or temporal events, whereas visual question answering usually requires surrounding context for recognition, comparison, or disambiguation. We therefore expand each spatial bounding box by scaling its width and height by 1.5 about its center, clipping the result to the image boundary. For temporal evidence, we extend each contiguous annotated segment by one frame at both ends. This context-preserving relaxation provides additional evidence without introducing excessive irrelevant visual content. We apply it only once before computing evidence coverage and constructing tool supervision. Finally, spatial and temporal annotations are converted into executable tool metadata under unified format. The resulting Reframe-100K supports both RL and OPD. 3.2. GD-GRPO We train spatial and temporal specialists independently on the image and video subsets of Reframe-100K using GDGRPO. The core idea is to couple observation acquisition with observation reliance. While observation rewards guide the policy toward informative tool actions, originalobservation dropout reduces its tendency to bypass the resulting observations, thereby establishing the necessity of the acquired observations. GD-GRPO is characterized by three key designs: reward, dropout, and subgroup. 3.2.1. Reward Design Outcome correctness alone cannot stably reveal whether tool retrieves relevant information or whether subsequent reasoning uses its returned observation. For an input = (Q, o0) consisting of question and its original observation, the reward is defined as R(τ ; x, p) = Rans(τ ; x) + (p)Rcall(τ ; x) + λobsRobs(τ ; x) Rpen(τ ; x), (1) where τ and [0, 1] denote trajectories and training progress, respectively. The four terms evaluate answer correctness, tool call behavior, grounding quality, and output validity, where the tool call term provides temporary exploration incentive derived from the annotation-based applicability. Both the valid-call bonus and the inapplicable-call Figure 2. Construction pipeline of Reframe-100K. We first collect public data sources and preprocess them into raw data pool. We then drop samples answerable from text alone, and audit the rest with 8 rollouts on the full input (F ) and on the annotated evidence alone (E), discarding samples that are (1) too easy or too hard; (2) insufficiently supported by their evidence. Remaining suspicious samples are diagnosed by Qwen and removed only when final reviewer confirms an answer or evidence error. design choices: (1) We restrict the toolset to two fundamental vision tools, CropImage and SelectFrames, for simplicity. (2) We adopt Qwen3.5-9B as our base model. (3) Both RL and OPD stages use the same data corpus. 3.1. Training Data Construction Reframe-100K comprises 63K image QA pairs and 37K video QA pairs, constructed from heterogeneous spatial and temporal grounding annotations. As illustrated in Fig. 2, we establish five-step cascaded data construction pipeline guided by the following three principles. Quality control of grounding annotations. The quality of grounding annotations is critical to our framework, as unreliable evidence can undermine both evidence-aware rewards and subsequent observation repair. We therefore place emphasis on evidence quality throughout our datacleaning pipeline, incorporating multiple rounds of evidence auditing and verification. As illustrated in Fig. 2, these procedures aim to ensure that the retained annotations provide reliable supervision for visual tool use. Data-centric tool applicability. Determining whether is beneficial remains challenging, particularly tool call when the model has not yet developed reliable tool-use capabilities. Unlike model-dependent strategies [33, 34], 3 Figure 3. Overview of GD-GRPO. The policy samples multi-turn tool-use rollouts. After the first successful tool call, the original input o0 is dropped with probability 0.5 while tool-returned observations ot remain visible, so the answer must rely on what the tools have retrieved. For images, we jointly match the cropped images along trajectory to the annotated regions using global one-to-one IoU matching, which rewards complementary coverage while preventing repeated localization of the same target from multiplying its reward. For videos, we evaluate the latest attempt using frame IoU rather than retrospectively selecting the most favorable attempt. Later attempts are discounted to encourage efficient acquisition. Importantly, grounding supervision is not gated by answer correctness. proper tool action receives credit even when the policy does not answer correctly. Examples without grounding annotations receive no Rcall or Robs, and remain supervised by answer correctness and validity penalties. 3.2.2. Original-Observation Dropout Accurate localization does not by itself establish observation reliance. model may still answer from the original visual input without using the tool-returned result. To reduce this bypass, we stochastically drop o0 with probability of 0.5 after the first successful tool call during training, while retaining the question, textual history, and tool-returned observations. The model then has to rely on the acquired observations for subsequent reasoning rather than bypassing them through the original input. At inference, the original visual input is always retained. Rather than prescribing tool actions, the dropout changes the conditions under which they contribute to successful reasoning. By removing the original visual input, it turns tool-returned observations from supplementary cues into essential information for subsequent reasoning. Coupled with grounding rewards, it encourages the policy to both acquire informative observations and genuinely rely on them. 3.2.3. Drop-Conditioned Subgroup Original-observation dropout introduces an external source of variation into rollout difficulty. Comparing dropped and retained trajectories against shared group baseline may encourage lower-quality trajectories, thereby confounding action quality with the randomly assigned condition. To address this, we compute relative advantages within subgroups that share the same pre-sampled dropout indicator di {0, 1}. For rollouts {τi} of input x, define Gx,d = {i : di = d}. (3) Crucially, subgroups are defined by the pre-sampled dropout indicator rather than actual dropout, ensuring that group assignment remains independent of the policys tooluse decisions. 4 The environment executes at and returns the corresponding observation, from which the student resumes sampling. Crucially, this selective intervention preserves wellgrounded student actions while repairing deficient ones, balancing on-policy exploration with observation validity. 3.3.2. Branch-Aware Distillation Observation repair introduces two distinct token sources: student-sampled tokens and injected action tokens I. For the former, we retain standard MOPD supervision, where the corresponding image or video specialist provides dense token-level feedback on the students actual continuation. Teacher routing follows the executed tool action, with the input modality providing the initial assignment. However, injected actions are not sampled from the student policy and should not be treated as on-policy tokens. We therefore introduce separate NLL objective: LOG-MOPD = LMOPD(S) + λbrLNLL(I), (cid:88) LNLL(I) = log πθ(yk hk), 1 kI (5) where hk denotes the interaction history preceding token yk. If there is no injected action, then the NLL term is omitted. This separation provides complementary supervision: NLL teaches the student how to reach informative observation states, while MOPD transfers expert behavior along the subsequent student-sampled trajectories. At inference, neither observation gating nor specialist teachers are required. Training details are provided in Appendix B. 4. Experiments 4.1. Experimental Setup Benchmarks. We evaluate Reframe on seven image benchmarks and seven video benchmarks, testing whether targeted visual inspection translates into both fine-grained perception and broader visual understanding. For images, [40], HR-Bench 4K/8K [35], VisualProbe [15], and ZoomBench [38] stress the ability to find and resolve task-relevant details within complex visual inputs. MMERealWorld [46] extends the evaluation to diverse real-world scenes, while PerceptionBench [21] probes atomic visual perception. For videos, Video-MME [8], Video-MMEv2 [9], MVBench [18], and MLVU [49] assess understanding across diverse tasks and temporal scales. MMEVideoOCR [30] and VSI-Bench [43] target video text understanding and spatial reasoning, respectively. V-STaR [3] probes spatial and temporal evidence understanding. Baselines. We conduct two groups of comparisons. The first compares training paradigms using five baselines: the modalityImage-RL and Video-RL, Qwen3.5-9B; specific specialists trained with GD-GRPO on singlemodality data; Mix-RL, trained with GD-GRPO on the Figure 4. Overview of OG-MOPD. Tool actions of the student policy are checked against annotated evidence using an IoU threshold. Missing, invalid, or poorly grounded actions are replaced with annotation-derived actions to obtain query-relevant Injected action tokens receive NLL supervision, observations. while retained student-generated tokens are trained with MOPD. Overall, GD-GRPO couples observation acquisition with downstream reliance: grounding rewards encourage the policy to acquire informative observations, while originalvision dropout promotes their actual use. This provides the foundation for observation-aligned capability consolidation in the subsequent OG-MOPD stage. 3.3. OG-MOPD For tool-use models, the effectiveness of distillation depends not only on the selected teacher but also on the observations available when its supervision is applied. deficient tool action can place the student in an uninformative visual state, constraining all subsequent teacher feedback. Although token-level optimization can improve future actions, feedback on the current continuation does not retroactively repair the observation already returned. OGMOPD therefore intervenes at the tool-action boundary to improve observation validity, while retaining the students generation. Essentially, this is trade-off between on-policy learning and observation validity. 3.3.1. For toolapplicable examples, we selectively replace missing, invalid, or poorly grounded actions according to (cid:40) at = , at is invalid or IoU(at, at, otherwise, ) < δ, (4) where δ is the grounding threshold. Missing actions are treated as invalid, and IoU is measured against the original or context-expanded annotations. 5 combined image and video data; and MOPD, which consolidates the two specialists through vanilla MOPD. The second compares Reframe with existing agentic visual reasoning models: Pixel-Reasoner, Thyme, DeepEyes, and DeepEyesV2, in terms of performance, observation dependence, and tool gain. Furthermore, outcome-based GRPO serves as baseline to diagnose the proposed GD-GRPO. Evaluation protocol. We evaluate all models under shared visual-token budgets using greedy decoding. Each original image receives up to 5,120 tokens, and each toolreturned image receives up to 1,960 tokens. For videos, we use 64 frames with 128 tokens per frame. Each selected frame receives up to 400 tokens, subject to cumulative budget of 4,096 tokens across all select calls. Evaluation details are provided in Appendix C. 4.2. Main Results Results are shown in Tables 2, 3 and 4. We make three main observations: (1) Reframe outperforms vanilla MOPD, which in turn outperforms Mix-RL. MOPD can even surpass its specialist teachers, while observation repair adds further gains; (2) Compared with outcome-based GRPO, GD-GRPO improves the specialists benchmark performance and increases observation dependence and tool gain; and (3) Reframe achieves the largest tool gain and the strongest dependence on tool-returned observations among the compared visual agents. 4.3. Ablation and Analysis We first examine GD-GRPO, then compare specialist consolidation methods, and finally analyze observation dependence and tool gain against existing agents. 4.3.1. Effectiveness of GD-GRPO Table 3 compares image specialists trained with GD-GRPO and outcome-based GRPO, which uses only correctness rewards and no original-observation dropout. GD-GRPO improves the image average by 2.07 points. In the toolgain evaluation, enabling tools adds 3.82 points with GDGRPO versus 1.97 with GRPO, while tool-free accuracy improves by only 0.22 points. These results suggest that GD-GRPO yields only modest gains in general visual capabilities, while its main benefit lies in enabling the model to translate visual tool use into better reasoning performance. To better understand this tool-related improvement, we examine how GD-GRPO changes the models response to different tool observations. GD-GRPO improves accuracy under GT, Random, and Blank by 5.23, 3.67, and 3.14 points, respectively, with the largest gain under GT. We summarize this behavior with the dependence score (Appendix C.2), defined as the fraction of errors under uninformative observations (the mean of Random and Blank) that are corrected once the ground-truth observation is supplied. It measures sensitivity to observation content rather than overall capability. GD-GRPO raises it from 52.59 to 69.03, while also improving accuracy under corrupted observations. Together with the larger tool gain, these results support better use of returned observations rather than greater vulnerability to misleading observations. 4.3.2. Comparison of Training Paradigms We compare Mix-RL, MOPD, and Reframe against the modality-specific experts in Table 2. Mix-RL falls short of the specialists. Mix-RL trails Image-RL and Video-RL in their respective modalities by 1.17 and 1.37 points  (Table 2)  , retaining 74% and 55% of their gains over the base model. Although it uses the GDGRPO reward, these signals are aggregated into trajectorylevel advantages rather than separate assessments of each acquisition and reasoning decision. The shared policy must therefore discover spatial and temporal strategies jointly, yet gradient updates favoring one modality do not necessarily benefit the other. This couples exploration across modalities with coarse credit assignment, providing plausible explanation for the specialist gap. In contrast, the MOPD results show that near-specialist performance in both modalities is attainable, suggesting that the learning process does matter. MOPD approaches specialist performance. MOPD retains 106% and 85% of the gains achieved by Image-RL and Video-RL, respectively. It surpasses both teachers on 5 of the 14 benchmarks. The key difference from Mix-RL lies in the supervision density. Mix-RL uses trajectorylevel advantage, while MOPD provides specialist feedback for each generated token. This gives the student more direct guidance on intermediate generation choices, reducing the need to infer their value from an aggregate response-level signal. Such dense supervision can make better use of each rollout, making MOPD more practical choice for consolidating specialists. Observation repair yields additional gains. With the same GD-GRPO specialists as teachers, Reframe improves over MOPD by 1.29 points on images and 0.78 on videos. The largest gain occurs on VisualProbe (+4.86). MOPD already teaches both actions and reasoning, but its feedback on continuation is conditioned on the observation the student has obtained. Repair provides task-relevant evidence before distillation continues. Its contribution is therefore focused on deficient actions in tool-applicable examples, complementing the broader consolidation already achieved by MOPD. The central trade-off in observation repair is between observation validity and the degree to which the rollout remains on-policy. An externally supplied action changes the history from which the student continues, even though the continuation itself remains student-generated. Tool gain complements the controlled-observation analysis by measuring the benefit of autonomous tool use. Across seven image benchmarks, tools improve Reframe from 64.25 to 69.48, gain of 5.23 points versus at most 1.47 for the other models. Relative to the tool-free Qwen3.5-9B (63.46), 87% of the overall gain stems from tool use, indicating that Reframes advantage largely arises from interaction with visual tools. Useful observations must be acquired through the models own actions. The larger tool gain, therefore, provides evidence that Reframe can combine evidence acquisition and use to improve its final answers. 5. Conclusion Reframe consolidates image and video reasoning predominantly through on-policy training. GD-GRPO encourages reliance on tool-returned observations through grounding rewards and original-input dropout, while OG-MOPD repairs deficient tool actions before continuing distillation. Across 14 benchmarks, Reframe improves over Mix-RL and vanilla MOPD, even surpassing both specialists. Diagnostic evaluations show stronger observation dependence and larger tool gains than the compared agentic visual models, highlighting the importance of both acquiring useful evidence and learning to use it.

Prompts and Tool Interface This section presents the system instructions, user-message format, tool definitions, and tool responses used in our experiments. The functions crop and select implement CropImage and SelectFrames, respectively. Upper-case placeholders denote sample-specific values. The <image> and <video> markers represent visual inputs expanded by the multimodal chat template. A.1. System Prompts Image-RL uses the image prompt and exposes only crop; Video-RL uses the video prompt and exposes only select. Mix-RL and the MOPD student use the unified prompt with both tools. The benchmark evaluator selects the image or video prompt according to the input modality. The tool-formatting instructions in Appendix A.3 precede these system instructions whenever tools are enabled. System prompt: image Answer the question using the images. Cropping is optional: use it only when closer view would clarify relevant details. Use at most 2 crop calls. Use stable 1based image IDs: original images are numbered in input order; crops have the IDs reported by the tool. Each bbox is [x_min,y_min,x_max,y_max] in integer 01000 coordinates of the target image: (0,0) is top-left and (1000,1000) is bottom-right. Use bbox_2d for one box or bboxes_2d for up to 3 distinct boxes, not both. Their total area must be at most 50% of the target image. multi-box call counts as one call. Avoid redundant boxes. Put only the final answer in boxed{...}, exactly once, with no text after it: an option letter for multiple choice, otherwise the shortest sufficient answer. System prompt: video Reason about the visual input and answer the question. Visual tools are optional. Use at most 2 visual operations. Call tool only when more focused spatial or temporal view is likely to improve grounding by concentrating relevant evidence and excluding distractors. If additional focusing is unlikely to improve reliability, answer directly without tool call. Preserve enough context to answer the full question; do not minimize the selected area or frame count at the expense of relevant evidence. For video input, use select only when smaller subset of frames would provide more relevant temporal evidence. Keep every relevant event segment with neighboring frame before and after it when available; do not fill unrelated gaps. When S1 tool is needed, follow the provided Qwen3.5 tool-call protocol, choose precise arguments, and continue reasoning from the returned visual evidence. End the response with exactly one final answer in boxed{...}, with no text after it. For multiple-choice questions, put only the option letter inside the box; for other questions, put only the shortest sufficient answer, without repeating the question. select arguments are {"target_frames": [<sorted unique 1-based frame indices>]}; each call must remove at least 50% of the current candidates. Keep original candidate-frame indices on later calls, and select strict subset of the previous selection. System prompt: unified imagevideo training Reason about the visual input and answer the question. Visual tools are optional. Use at most 2 visual operations. Call tool only when more focused spatial or temporal view is likely to improve grounding by concentrating relevant evidence and excluding distractors. If additional focusing is unlikely to improve reliability, answer directly without tool call. Preserve enough context to answer the full question; do not minimize the selected area or frame count at the expense of relevant evidence. For image or multi-image input, use crop only when the question-relevant evidence is spatially localized and focusing it is likely to clarify fine details or reduce distracting context. Include small spatial margin and any nearby objects or labels needed to interpret the evidence. For video input, use select only when smaller subset of frames would provide more relevant temporal evidence. Keep every relevant event segment with neighboring frame before and after it when available; do not fill unrelated gaps. When tool is needed, follow the provided Qwen3.5 tool-call protocol, choose precise arguments, and continue reasoning from the returned visual evidence. End the response with exactly one final answer in boxed{...}, with no text after it. For multiplechoice questions, put only the option letter inside the box; for other questions, put only the shortest sufficient answer, without repeating the question. select arguments are {"tar- [<sorted unique 1-based frame indices>]}; get_frames": each call must remove at least 50% of the current candidates. Keep original candidate-frame indices on later calls, and select strict subset of the previous selection. crop arguments are {"target_image": <1-based integer>, "bbox_2d": [x_min,y_min,x_max,y_max]}, or replace bbox_2d with "bboxes_2d": [[x_min,y_min,x_max,y_max], ...] for up to 3 distinct boxes. multi-box call returns one image per box and counts as one operation. Each returned crop has its own visual-token budget. Do not include unrelated or redundant boxes; these are penalized. Coordinates use the integer 01000 coordinate grid: (0,0) is top-left and (1000,1000) is bottom-right; all boxes in one call must together retain at most 50% of the source image area. Use the stable image IDs reported by tools. For video with no image inputs or returned images yet, target_image indexes the original candidate frames. For tool-free evaluation, the tool definitions are omitted and the system instruction is replaced with the following text. System prompt: without tools Reason about the visual input and answer the question without calling tools. Put the final answer in boxed{}. A.2. User Messages and Frame Indices The question is taken from the corresponding training example or prepared benchmark record, including its answer choices and any task-specific answer format instruction. Reference answers and grounding annotations are not appended to the question. Training and evaluation use one image marker per input image, in the supplied order. User message: images <image>...<image>{QUESTION} User message: video training and evaluation <video>{QUESTION} During video training, the system prompt includes the following frame-index instruction for select. Indices refer to sampled frames; timestamps in the template are synthetic. Frame indices for video training The candidate timeline has {N} frames, numbered 1..{N} in order. target_frames uses these candidate indices, not seconds or raw-video frame numbers. Time markers such as <1.2 seconds> are synthetic, spacing candidate frames 0.5 seconds apart; they are not real video time. A.3. Tool Prompt and Function Definitions The Qwen3.5 chat template places the function definitions and invocation instructions before the modality-specific system prompt. The template below is shared across tool-enabled settings: {TOOL_DEFINITIONS} is replaced by the JSON definitions of the enabled tools, and {SYSTEM_PROMPT} by the corresponding text above. The unified setting lists select followed by crop; the specialist settings include only their respective tool. Shared tool prompt: Qwen3.5 format # Tools You have access to the following functions: <tools> {TOOL_DEFINITIONS} </tools> If you choose to call function ONLY reply in the following format with NO suffix: <tool_call> <function=example_function_name> <parameter=example_parameter_1> value_1 </parameter> <parameter=example_parameter_2> This is the value for the second parameter that can span multiple lines </parameter> </function> </tool_call> <IMPORTANT> Reminder: - Function calls MUST follow the specified format: an inner <function=...></function> block must be nested within <tool_call></ tool_call> XML tags - Required parameters MUST be specified - You may provide optional reasoning for your function call in natural language BEFORE the function call, but NOT after - If there is no function call available, answer the question like normal with your current knowledge and do not tell the user about function calls </IMPORTANT> {SYSTEM_PROMPT}

Semantic Evaluation Prompt The generic semantic scorer receives the question, reference answer, and model answer as text. Its prompt is separate from the policys interaction: reference answers are visible to the scorer only. Benchmark-specific scorers, including the spatial and temporal metrics of V-STaR, use their own scoring rules. Semantic judge: user message {"q":"{QUESTION}","r":"{REFERENCE_ANSWER}"," a":"{MODEL_ANSWER}"} B. Training Details Tables 5 and 6 summarize the training configurations used in our experiments. Both stages initialize the trainable language model from Qwen3.5-9B and keep the visual encoder and multimodal aligner frozen. Image-RL and Video-RL use their respective modality subsets, while Mix-RL and the distillation student use the mixed training set. GD-GRPO uses Dr.GRPO-style fixed-length normalization, dividing each turns token-loss sum by 2,048 while retaining the trajectory and distributed weights. Advantages are standardized within the pre-sampled originalobservation drop/keep subgroups, with dropout probability 0.5. The KL reference remains fixed at the base model. MOPD uses the specialists token-level feedback without an additional fixed-base KL term or the handcrafted RL rewards. Its teacher log-probability differences are clipped to [5, 5]. Injected actions in OG-MOPD receive the separate NLL term with coefficient 1. Original-observation dropout is disabled during distillation. The call bonus and inapplicable-call penalty are multiplied by (p) for both images and videos. valid call earns the bonus once per applicable trajectory, while each attempted call on an inapplicable example incurs the call penalty. The validity and failed-call penalties in Table 5 are positive magnitudes subtracted through Rpen. The validity penalty applies to each invalid action and once to an invalid final answer. Failed executions and unknown tool names use the failed-call penalty instead. An inaccurate but otherwise valid localization reduces the evidence reward without incurring validity penalty. The first crop attempt has weight 1, and boxes from later attempts have weight 0.85 in the joint matching score. For frame selection, only the latest attempt is scored, with factor of 0.85 if more than one call was attempted. The discount is applied once rather than compounded, and failed attempts count toward the attempt order. Specialist training uses 32 GPUs, while distillation uses eight GPUs. Student rollout generation is colocated with training. Mix-RL follows the GD-GRPO batch configuration and uses temperature 1, top-p = 0.95, and no top-k S4 Table 5. Optimization and reward settings. Observation gate. We train all models for one epoch and select the best-performing checkpoints. The Image-RL and Video-RL checkpoints serve as teachers for distillation. Observation-dependence Study The study uses the 191 multiple-choice questions of V, with one sample per question under each of five conditions. In Direct, the model answers without tools. In Natural, the model chooses its own tool actions. For each model and question, the three controlled conditions share an injected canonical crop action, the same pre-continuation text, and the same tool-response text. Only the returned image content changes. Each controlled tool response ends with the same instruction: This was your only tool call. Answer the question now from the images above, without calling any more tools. GT: the annotated target region, with the contextpreserving expansion used to construct the canonical crop. Random: same-size crop at different location in the original image, using question-dependent random seed. Blank: same-size constant gray image, with RGB value (128, 128, 128). All three returned images use the same resizing and visualtoken budget. Random crops target IoU at most 0.1 with GT. If none of 100 sampled positions meets this target, we choose the lowest-IoU position among the samples and four image corners. The full original image remains visible in all five conditions. After the controlled observation is inserted, the model generates one continuation and no further tool action is executed. Attempts to call tool again are logged separately.
